claim: Ataxia Telangiectasia (A-T) is a rare disorder occurring in approximately one in 100,000 individuals.
source: Ataxia Telangiectasia (A-T) is a rare (one in ~100,000) (Swift et al., 1986), autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by cancer predisposition, immune deficiency, and a highly penetrant progressive and severe ataxia linked to cerebellar atrophy (Rothblum-Oviatt et al., 2016; Boder and Sedgwick, 1958; Levy and Lang, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Swift et al., 1986, which provides epidemiological data on A-T prevalence.

claim: A-T is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder.
source: Ataxia Telangiectasia (A-T) is a rare (one in ~100,000) (Swift et al., 1986), autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by cancer predisposition, immune deficiency, and a highly penetrant progressive and severe ataxia linked to cerebellar atrophy (Rothblum-Oviatt et al., 2016; Boder and Sedgwick, 1958; Levy and Lang, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple sources (Rothblum-Oviatt et al., 2016; Boder and Sedgwick, 1958; Levy and Lang, 2018) that characterize A-T as autosomal recessive.

claim: A-T is characterized by cancer predisposition, immune deficiency, and progressive ataxia linked to cerebellar atrophy.
source: Ataxia Telangiectasia (A-T) is a rare (one in ~100,000) (Swift et al., 1986), autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by cancer predisposition, immune deficiency, and a highly penetrant progressive and severe ataxia linked to cerebellar atrophy (Rothblum-Oviatt et al., 2016; Boder and Sedgwick, 1958; Levy and Lang, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rothblum-Oviatt et al., 2016; Boder and Sedgwick, 1958; Levy and Lang, 2018, which describe the clinical features of A-T.

claim: A-T patients typically die in their second or third decade of life.
source: A-T patients typically die in their second or third decade of life (Crawford et al., 2006) from lymphatic cancers, respiratory infections, or complications of ataxia—unfortunately, survivability has not dramatically changed since the 1950s (Micol et al., 2011; Rothblum-Oviatt et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Crawford et al., 2006, which provides data on A-T patient survival.

claim: A-T patients die from lymphatic cancers, respiratory infections, or complications of ataxia.
source: A-T patients typically die in their second or third decade of life (Crawford et al., 2006) from lymphatic cancers, respiratory infections, or complications of ataxia—unfortunately, survivability has not dramatically changed since the 1950s (Micol et al., 2011; Rothblum-Oviatt et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Crawford et al., 2006; Micol et al., 2011; Rothblum-Oviatt et al., 2016, which describe causes of death in A-T patients.

claim: Survivability of A-T patients has not dramatically changed since the 1950s.
source: A-T patients typically die in their second or third decade of life (Crawford et al., 2006) from lymphatic cancers, respiratory infections, or complications of ataxia—unfortunately, survivability has not dramatically changed since the 1950s (Micol et al., 2011; Rothblum-Oviatt et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Micol et al., 2011; Rothblum-Oviatt et al., 2016, which provide historical data on A-T patient survival.

claim: Progressive decline in motor coordination has the greatest negative impact on A-T patient quality of life.
source: While disease progression and cause of death vary widely across patients, the highly penetrant progressive decline in motor coordination is reported as having the greatest negative impact on a patient's quality of life (Jackson et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jackson et al., 2016, which reports on quality of life impacts in A-T patients.

claim: No long-term therapies are available for treating ataxia and associated cerebellar dysfunction in A-T.
source: Care is generally palliative, directed at reducing, limiting, or eliminating cancers or infections. No long-term therapies are available for treating the ataxia and associated cerebellar dysfunction and atrophy.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text as a current limitation in A-T treatment.

claim: A-T is caused by deficiency or dysfunction of the ATM protein.
source: A-T is caused by deficiency or dysfunction of the ATM (A-T mutated) protein (Savitsky et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Savitsky et al., 1995, which identified ATM as the gene responsible for A-T.

claim: Premature termination codon (PTC) causing nonsense mutations account for up to half of known A-T cases.
source: Premature termination codon (PTC) causing nonsense mutations account for up to a half of known cases, with missense and deletion mutations also contributing (Concannon and Gatti, 1997; Sandoval et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Concannon and Gatti, 1997; Sandoval et al., 1999, which characterize the types of mutations causing A-T.

claim: ATM is a serine/threonine PIKK family kinase that plays a key role in the DNA damage response.
source: ATM is a serine/threonine PIKK family kinase that plays a key role in the DNA damage response (DDR), protecting cells from the tens of thousands of DNA lesions incurred each day (Lindahl and Barnes, 2000; Kastan and Bartek, 2004; Shiloh and Ziv, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lindahl and Barnes, 2000; Kastan and Bartek, 2004; Shiloh and Ziv, 2013, which describe ATM's biochemical properties and function.

claim: Cells incur tens of thousands of DNA lesions each day.
source: ATM is a serine/threonine PIKK family kinase that plays a key role in the DNA damage response (DDR), protecting cells from the tens of thousands of DNA lesions incurred each day (Lindahl and Barnes, 2000; Kastan and Bartek, 2004; Shiloh and Ziv, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lindahl and Barnes, 2000, which provides data on the frequency of DNA damage.

claim: In the active monomeric form, ATM phosphorylates several key proteins to halt DNA production and initiate cell cycle arrest.
source: In the active monomeric form, ATM phosphorylates several key proteins halting the production of new DNA (cell cycle arrest) (Ando et al., 2012), and then, depending on severity of the damage, initiates DNA repair or programmed cell death (i.e., apoptosis) (Ando et al., 2012; Rashi-Elkeles et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ando et al., 2012; Rashi-Elkeles et al., 2006, which describe ATM's role in cell cycle regulation.

claim: ATM initiates DNA repair or apoptosis depending on the severity of DNA damage.
source: In the active monomeric form, ATM phosphorylates several key proteins halting the production of new DNA (cell cycle arrest) (Ando et al., 2012), and then, depending on severity of the damage, initiates DNA repair or programmed cell death (i.e., apoptosis) (Ando et al., 2012; Rashi-Elkeles et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ando et al., 2012; Rashi-Elkeles et al., 2006, which describe ATM's role in DNA damage response.

claim: Downstream DDR pathway targets of ATM include p53, CHK2, BRCA1, SMC1, and NBS1.
source: Several downstream DDR pathway targets of ATM have been identified, including p53, CHK2, BRCA1, SMC1, and NBS1 (Matsuoka et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Matsuoka et al., 2007, which identified ATM phosphorylation targets.

claim: ATM contributes to recombination during gene rearrangement in T- and B-lymphocyte maturation.
source: ATM's role in DNA repair is also implicated in normal immune system development, where it is proposed to contribute to the recombination of natural DNA splicing that occurs during gene rearrangement in T- and B-lymphocyte maturation (Chao et al., 2000; Matei et al., 2006; Vacchio et al., 2007; Schubert et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chao et al., 2000; Matei et al., 2006; Vacchio et al., 2007; Schubert et al., 2002, which describe ATM's role in immune development.

claim: ATM has been implicated in oxidative stress homeostasis.
source: Although its roles are still emerging, ATM has also been implicated in oxidative stress homeostasis (Guo et al., 2010) and mitophagy (Valentin-Vega and Kastan, 2012; Pizzamiglio et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2010, which describes ATM's role in oxidative stress.

claim: ATM has been implicated in mitophagy.
source: Although its roles are still emerging, ATM has also been implicated in oxidative stress homeostasis (Guo et al., 2010) and mitophagy (Valentin-Vega and Kastan, 2012; Pizzamiglio et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Valentin-Vega and Kastan, 2012; Pizzamiglio et al., 2020, which describe ATM's role in mitophagy.

claim: Multiple DNA damage response proteins besides ATM are linked to ataxia, including APTX, MRE11, NBS1, SETX, and TDP1.
source: It is unclear why ATM deficiency causes ataxia, but it is far from the only DDR protein linked to ataxia, as Aprataxin (APTX) (Aicardi et al., 1988), Meiotic recombination 11 homolog 1 (MRE11) (Sedghi et al., 2018), Nibrin (NBS1) (van der Burgt et al., 1996), Senataxin (SETX) (Moreira et al., 2004), and Tyrosyl-DNA Phosphodiesterase 1 (TDP1) (Takashima et al., 2002) when absent or dysfunctional can cause cerebellar-related ataxia.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aicardi et al., 1988; Sedghi et al., 2018; van der Burgt et al., 1996; Moreira et al., 2004; Takashima et al., 2002, which link these proteins to ataxia.

claim: The neurological features of genome instability syndromes may have a common underlying cause.
source: This suggests that the neurological features of genome instability syndromes have a common underlying cause, although this has yet to be mechanistically demonstrated (McKinnon, 2009; Rass et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McKinnon, 2009; Rass et al., 2007, which discuss commonalities in genome instability syndromes.

claim: Several A-T rodent models have been created but none develop overt, progressive ataxia with cerebellar dysfunction and atrophy.
source: Several A-T rodent models have been created over the past several years by inserting gene mutations that cause protein dysfunction (lack kinase activity) or complete deficiency (Herzog et al., 1998; Xu and Baltimore, 1996; Elson et al., 1996; Spring et al., 2001; Campbell et al., 2015; Quek et al., 2016; Tal et al., 2018; Lavin, 2013); a minipig was also recently reported (Beraldi et al., 2017). However, none develop an overt, progressive ataxia with cerebellar dysfunction and atrophy that recapitulates the human disease, even though other aspects of the disorder like thyroid cancers, infertility, and immune abnormalities do develop.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Herzog et al., 1998; Xu and Baltimore, 1996; Elson et al., 1996; Spring et al., 2001; Campbell et al., 2015; Quek et al., 2016; Tal et al., 2018; Lavin, 2013; Beraldi et al., 2017) describing prior A-T animal models.

claim: Prior A-T animal models develop thyroid cancers, infertility, and immune abnormalities.
source: Several A-T rodent models have been created over the past several years by inserting gene mutations that cause protein dysfunction (lack kinase activity) or complete deficiency (Herzog et al., 1998; Xu and Baltimore, 1996; Elson et al., 1996; Spring et al., 2001; Campbell et al., 2015; Quek et al., 2016; Tal et al., 2018; Lavin, 2013); a minipig was also recently reported (Beraldi et al., 2017). However, none develop an overt, progressive ataxia with cerebellar dysfunction and atrophy that recapitulates the human disease, even though other aspects of the disorder like thyroid cancers, infertility, and immune abnormalities do develop.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies describing phenotypes in prior A-T animal models.

claim: Species-specific molecular compensations in mice may provide redundancies that minimize effects of ATM deficiency in the brain.
source: It is possible that species-specific molecular compensations in mice provide redundancies or alternative pathways minimizing the effects of ATM deficiency in the brain (El-Brolosy and Stainier, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to El-Brolosy and Stainier, 2017, which discusses genetic compensation mechanisms.

claim: The shortened lifespan of prior A-T models may be too brief for stochastic mechanisms driving cerebellar dysfunction to accumulate.
source: It is also possible that the shortened lifespan of prior models (Barlow et al., 1996) is too brief for the stochastic mechanisms driving cerebellar dysfunction and atrophy to accumulate and impact motor behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barlow et al., 1996, which describes the lifespan of prior A-T models.

claim: Low levels of ATM protein or active fragments with residual kinase activity may limit neuropathology in prior models.
source: Other challenges include potentially leaky genetic manipulations that result in low levels of ATM protein or active fragments with residual kinase activity, thus limiting neuropathology (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2011, which discusses limitations of prior genetic models.

claim: APTX deficiency causes ataxia with ocular apraxia type 1 (AOA1) in humans.
source: We chose to additionally knockout Aptx because its deficiency causes an A-T like disorder in humans called ataxia with ocular apraxia type 1 (AOA1), which does not feature A-T's other system defects that could increase the potential for prenatal lethality or early death (e.g., immunodeficiency and cancer predisposition) (Coutinho et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Coutinho et al., 2002, which describes AOA1.

claim: AOA1 does not feature immunodeficiency and cancer predisposition like A-T.
source: We chose to additionally knockout Aptx because its deficiency causes an A-T like disorder in humans called ataxia with ocular apraxia type 1 (AOA1), which does not feature A-T's other system defects that could increase the potential for prenatal lethality or early death (e.g., immunodeficiency and cancer predisposition) (Coutinho et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Coutinho et al., 2002, which characterizes AOA1 clinical features.

claim: APTX is a phosphodiesterase involved in DNA reassembly after double- and single-stranded repair.
source: Moreover, APTX is a phosphodiesterase involved in DNA reassembly after double- and single-stranded repair, and has a function downstream of—but not directly regulated by or related to—ATM (Gueven et al., 2004; Schellenberg et al., 2015; Ahel et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gueven et al., 2004; Schellenberg et al., 2015; Ahel et al., 2006, which describe APTX function.

claim: APTX has a function downstream of but not directly regulated by ATM.
source: Moreover, APTX is a phosphodiesterase involved in DNA reassembly after double- and single-stranded repair, and has a function downstream of—but not directly regulated by or related to—ATM (Gueven et al., 2004; Schellenberg et al., 2015; Ahel et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gueven et al., 2004; Schellenberg et al., 2015; Ahel et al., 2006, which describe the relationship between APTX and ATM.

claim: Mice deficient in both ATM and APTX develop cerebellar dysfunction, atrophy, and progressive ataxia.
source: Our results indeed demonstrate that mice deficient in ATM and APTX develop cerebellar dysfunction, atrophy, and a progressive and profound ataxia, while mice deficient in either protein alone do not.
evidence: The claim is stated as a result of the study and is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mice deficient in either ATM or APTX alone do not develop ataxia.
source: Our results indeed demonstrate that mice deficient in ATM and APTX develop cerebellar dysfunction, atrophy, and a progressive and profound ataxia, while mice deficient in either protein alone do not.
evidence: The claim is stated as a result of the study and is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Double mutant mice display defects in immune maturation and high incidence of thymomas.
source: Additionally, double mutants displayed other characteristic symptoms of A-T, including defects in immune maturation and a high incidence of cancer (thymomas), making it the most representative model, from a phenotypic standpoint, to date.
evidence: The claim is stated as a result of the study and is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The c.103C>T mutation in the Atm gene is common to a large family of North African A-T patients.
source: Thus, we inserted a PTC-causing nonsense mutation (103C>T) in the Atm gene common to a large family of North African A-T patients (Gilad et al., 1996a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gilad et al., 1996a, which describes this mutation in A-T patients.

claim: The c.103C>T mutation results in a premature termination codon at amino acid 35.
source: This mutation results in a PTC at what would normally be amino acid 35 and the loss of ATM translation.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text describing the mutation.

claim: Small Molecule Read-Through compounds can restore ATM production in mice with nonsense mutations.
source: Here, we report proof-of-principle experiments demonstrating that clinically relevant genetic mutations incorporated into the A-T mouse model are amenable to read-through compounds and thus appropriate for preclinical testing of SMRT compounds.
evidence: The claim is stated as a result of the study and is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice grew approximately 55% slower than control genotypes.
source: We found that AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice grew ~55% slower and reached estimated plateau weights that were ~35% less than control genotypes (log-rank, n=21–40, p<0.0001; Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of growth data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice reached plateau weights approximately 35% less than control genotypes.
source: We found that AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice grew ~55% slower and reached estimated plateau weights that were ~35% less than control genotypes (log-rank, n=21–40, p<0.0001; Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of growth data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: No significant weight differences were detected across genotypes at postnatal day 8.
source: These differences in weight were a postnatal phenomenon, as no significant weight differences were detected just after birth (P8) across all genotypes (one-way ANOVA, n=5–23, p>0.23).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA) of weight data at P8.

claim: Adolescent male double mutant mice at P45 weighed on average 30% less than wild-type mice.
source: Adolescent double mutant mice at postnatal day 45 (P45) weighed on average 30% less in male mice (double mutant: 14.4±1.0 g [n=13] vs. wild-type: 20.2±0.5 g [n=16], t-test, p<0.0001) and 25% less in females (double mutant: 12.7±0.6 g [n=17] vs. wild-type: 17.0±0.2 g [n=15], t-test, p<0.0001; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of weight data at P45.

claim: Adolescent female double mutant mice at P45 weighed on average 25% less than wild-type mice.
source: Adolescent double mutant mice at postnatal day 45 (P45) weighed on average 30% less in male mice (double mutant: 14.4±1.0 g [n=13] vs. wild-type: 20.2±0.5 g [n=16], t-test, p<0.0001) and 25% less in females (double mutant: 12.7±0.6 g [n=17] vs. wild-type: 17.0±0.2 g [n=15], t-test, p<0.0001; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of weight data at P45.

claim: 53% of AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice were still alive at 400 days of age.
source: Survivability of the AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice was significantly reduced compared to Atm+/+; Aptx+/+ mice, with 53% of mice still alive at 400 days of age, compared to 97% of Atm+/+; Aptx+/+ mice at the same time point (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: 97% of Atm+/+; Aptx+/+ mice were still alive at 400 days of age.
source: Survivability of the AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice was significantly reduced compared to Atm+/+; Aptx+/+ mice, with 53% of mice still alive at 400 days of age, compared to 97% of Atm+/+; Aptx+/+ mice at the same time point (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: ATM deficiency alone was sufficient to reduce survivability in mice.
source: ATM deficiency alone was sufficient to reduce survivability; as compared to Atm+/+; Aptx+/+ mice, both AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx+/+ and AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx+/− had significantly reduced survivability (42%, log-rank, χ2(1, 56)=13.49, p=0.0002% and 52%, log-rank, χ2(1, 53)=19.54, p<0.0001, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (log-rank test) of survival data.

claim: No significant difference in survivability was detected between ATM-deficient mice with partial or complete APTX deficiency.
source: No significant difference in survivability between ATM-deficient mice with partial or complete APTX deficiency was detected (log-rank, χ2(2, 85)=1.01, p=0.6).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (log-rank test) of survival data.

claim: Mice harboring at least one functional copy of the Atm gene had normal survivability regardless of APTX expression.
source: Conversely, mice harboring at least one functional copy of the Atm gene had normal survivability, regardless of whether they expressed APTX or not (log-rank, χ2(3, 131)=3.08, p=0.4).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (log-rank test) of survival data.

claim: A third of ATM-deficient mice died from complications related to large thymic cancers.
source: Generally, a third of mice with ATM deficiency died from complications related to large thymic cancers (thymoma) found in the thoracic cavity (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by postmortem necropsy data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The presence or absence of APTX did not impact cancer prevalence in ATM-deficient mice.
source: The presence or absence of APTX did not impact cancer prevalence, and mice with at least one Atm transcript were cancer-free up until at least P400.
evidence: The claim is supported by cancer incidence data from the study.

claim: Mice with at least one Atm transcript were cancer-free up until at least P400.
source: The presence or absence of APTX did not impact cancer prevalence, and mice with at least one Atm transcript were cancer-free up until at least P400.
evidence: The claim is supported by cancer incidence data from the study.

claim: Motor coordination deficits emerge between 210 and 400 days after birth in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice.
source: Overall, we find motor coordination deficits emerge between 210 and 400 days after birth in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice and find no evidence of ataxia in mice with at least one copy of the Atm or Aptx gene (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figures 3A and B.

claim: No evidence of ataxia was found in mice with at least one copy of the Atm or Aptx gene.
source: Overall, we find motor coordination deficits emerge between 210 and 400 days after birth in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice and find no evidence of ataxia in mice with at least one copy of the Atm or Aptx gene (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figures 3A and B.

claim: AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice at P400 took twice as long to descend the vertical pole compared to control mice.
source: For the vertical pole test, AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice took twice as long to descend at P400 compared to Atm+/+; Aptx+/+, Atm+/+; Aptx−/−, AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx+/+, or AtmR35X/+; Aptx−/− mice (Male: 29.1 ± 0.9 s [n=3] vs. 7.5 ± 0.4 s [n=12], 12.5±2.5 s [n=9], 9.2±0.9 s [n=10], 8.6±0.9 s [n=11], one-way ANOVA, F(4, 40)=19.9, p<0.0001; Female: 19.0±4.0 s [n=4] vs. 7.5±0.4 s [n=12], 7.8 ± 0.4 s [n=10], 10.5±1.2 s [n=6], 8.2±0.5 s [n = 8], one-way ANOVA, F(4, 35)=13.9, p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA) of vertical pole test data.

claim: AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice at P400 spend twice as much time with three paws in contact with the ground during ambulation compared to control mice.
source: An examination of gait indicated that AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice at P400, but not P210 need additional stabilization during ambulation, as they spend twice as much time with three paws, rather than the normal 2, in contact with the ground as they walk across the gait analysis platform (Male: 56.2% vs. 26.4–32.2%, one-way ANOVA, F(4, 54)=14.3, p<0.0001; Female: 58.4% vs. 18.9–28.8%, one-way ANOVA, F(3, 178)=95.5, p<0.0001; Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA) of gait data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice display slower cadence and average speed at P400 compared to control genotypes.
source: AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− also display a slower cadence and average speed across the platform compared to all other genotypes at P400 (cadence, Male: 9.5 vs. 13.3–15.9 steps/s, one-way ANOVA, F(3, 204)=36.8, p<0.0001; Female: 9.1 vs. 14.2–15.9 steps/s, one-way ANOVA, F(3, 204)=39.7, p<0.0001; speed, Male: 8.8 vs. 22–26 cm/s, one-way ANOVA, F(4, 50)=28.3, p<0.0001; Female: 58.4 vs. 18.9–28.8 cm/s, one-way ANOVA, F(3, 178)=39.7, p<0.0001; Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 3–1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA) of gait data.

claim: Motor deficits were first detected at P8 in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice using the righting reflex test.
source: We first detected differences in motor function at P8, where AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice took 3–4 times longer on average to right themselves compared to Atm+/+; Aptx+/+ mice (Male: 6.4±1.1 s [n=24] vs. 1.5±0.1 s [n=23], t-test, p<0.0002; Female: 11.1±1.9 s [n=21] vs. 2.4±0.3 s [n=17], t-test, p<0.0002; Figure 3C bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of righting reflex data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice took 3-4 times longer to right themselves at P8 compared to wild-type mice.
source: We first detected differences in motor function at P8, where AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice took 3–4 times longer on average to right themselves compared to Atm+/+; Aptx+/+ mice (Male: 6.4±1.1 s [n=24] vs. 1.5±0.1 s [n=23], t-test, p<0.0002; Female: 11.1±1.9 s [n=21] vs. 2.4±0.3 s [n=17], t-test, p<0.0002; Figure 3C bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of righting reflex data.

claim: Significant differences between AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− and wild-type mice were detected at 30 days of age in behavioral tests measuring body position and spontaneous activity.
source: At 30 days of age, we detected significant differences between AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− and Atm+/+; Aptx+/+ mice in behavioral tests that qualitatively measure body position and spontaneous activity (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by SHIRPA behavioral data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Striking differences in behavior related to movement were observed in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice at P400.
source: Striking differences in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− compared to Atm+/+; Aptx+/+ mice were observed at P400, especially for behaviors related to movement, including locomotor activity, body position, and gait (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by SHIRPA behavioral data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Purkinje neurons from AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice had significantly higher membrane input resistance than those from wild-type mice.
source: PNs recorded from AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice had significantly 'tighter' membranes, displaying higher membrane input resistances (Rm) than those from Atm+/+; Aptx+/+ mice (47.7±5.6 [n=15] vs. 30.2±1.47 [n=23] MΩ, t-test, p=0.008; Figure 4B) and displayed a faster membrane time constant (τ) (3.6±0.4 [n=15] vs. 5.1±0.3 [n=23] ms, t-test, p=0.009; Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Purkinje neurons from AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice displayed a faster membrane time constant than those from wild-type mice.
source: PNs recorded from AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice had significantly 'tighter' membranes, displaying higher membrane input resistances (Rm) than those from Atm+/+; Aptx+/+ mice (47.7±5.6 [n=15] vs. 30.2±1.47 [n=23] MΩ, t-test, p=0.008; Figure 4B) and displayed a faster membrane time constant (τ) (3.6±0.4 [n=15] vs. 5.1±0.3 [n=23] ms, t-test, p=0.009; Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: The total membrane capacitance of AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− Purkinje neurons is significantly reduced compared to wild-type.
source: These results indicate that the total membrane capacitance (Cm=τ/Rm) of the AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− PNs is significantly reduced (98.25±19.23 [n=15] vs. 175.6±12.67 [n=23] pF, t-test, p=0.0025; Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of calculated membrane capacitance data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Reduced membrane capacitance suggests ATM- and APTX-deficient Purkinje neurons have less or thinner membranes than wild-type.
source: At the cellular level, this suggests that the ATM- and APTX-deficient PNs have less (i.e., decreased area) or thinner membranes than that of wild-type PNs, a result suggestive of a developmental deficit or neurodegenerative process (Dell'Orco et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the membrane capacitance data, supported by a citation to Dell'Orco et al., 2015.

claim: Significant deficits in the ability of Purkinje neurons to fire continuously in response to current injection were observed in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice.
source: Significant deficits in the ability of PNs to fire continuously in response to current injection were observed in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Action potentials in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− Purkinje neurons have lower amplitude, higher threshold, and smaller area compared to wild-type.
source: These deficits were associated with significant perturbations in the amplitude, threshold, and area of evoked APs (amplitude: 66.2±0.7 [n=14] vs. 72.1±1.4 [n=13] ΔmV, t-test, p=0.003; threshold: –55.2±1.5 to –48.61±1.9 mV, t-test, p=0.0196; area: 17.96±0.6 vs. 20.63±1.0 mV*ms, t-test, p=0.048; Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of action potential properties presented in Figure 4C.

claim: No difference in spontaneous EPSC size was detected between AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− and wild-type Purkinje neurons.
source: No difference in sEPSC size was detected, indicating the function of granule cell axon terminals (i.e., parallel fibers) was relatively normal in the AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− cerebellum (18.92±1.3 [n=11] vs. 23.4±3.3 [n=11] pA, t-test, p=0.477; Figure 4D, Yamasaki et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of sEPSC data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: Spontaneous EPSC frequency was significantly increased in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− Purkinje neurons compared to wild-type.
source: sEPSC frequency, however, was found to be significantly increased, a phenomenon that could be attributed to either an increase in the total number of synapses, an increase in the size of the readily releasable pool of synaptic vesicles, or an increase in the probability of neurotransmitter release in PNs of AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice (18.75±2.8 Hz [n=11] vs. 11.4±1.0 Hz [n=11], t-test, p=0.047; Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of sEPSC frequency data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: Parallel fiber synaptic properties were normal in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice, showing no significant differences in short-term facilitation.
source: The synaptic properties of parallel fibers were found to be normal, displaying no significant differences in the expected short-term facilitation (Atluri and Regehr, 1996) or halfwidth and decay time constant of the evoked EPSC (PPR: 1.3±0.03 [n=10] vs. 1.4±0.05 [n=13], t-test, p=0.162; halfwidth: 3.9±0.6 vs. 4.9±0.4 ms, t-test, p=0.175; time constant: 3.5±0.5 vs. 4.7±0.4 ms, t-test, p=0.054; Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of parallel fiber synaptic data presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Climbing fiber-to-Purkinje neuron synaptic responses showed significantly greater pair-pulse depression in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice.
source: In comparison, we found climbing fiber-to-PN synaptic responses, which normally display pair-pulse depression (Hansel and Linden, 2000), to depress at significantly greater magnitudes in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice (PPR: 0.6±0.03 [n=6] vs. 0.7±0.02 [n=9], t-test, p=0.03; Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of climbing fiber synaptic data presented in Figure 4F.

claim: The halfwidth and decay time constant of climbing fiber evoked currents were smaller in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice.
source: The overall width and decay time constant of the evoked currents were also smaller (halfwidth: 2.3±0.6 [n=6] vs. 3.0±0.2 [n=9] ms, t-test, p=0.004; time constant (fast): 1.1±0.14 vs. 2.9±0.4 ms, t-test, [p=0.001]).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of climbing fiber EPSC kinetics.

claim: Decreased rates of spontaneous Purkinje neuron action potential firing have been observed in several mouse models of ataxia.
source: Decreased rates of spontaneous PN AP firing, which can be indicative of PN dysfunction, have been observed in several mouse models of ataxia, including spinocerebellar ataxias (SCA) 2, 3, 5, 6, 13, and 27, several models of episodic ataxia (e.g., leaner, ducky, and tottering), and autosomal-recessive spastic ataxia of the Charlevoix-Saguenay (Hourez et al., 2011; Hansen et al., 2013; Dell'Orco et al., 2017; Kasumu and Bezprozvanny, 2012; Liu et al., 2009; Perkins et al., 2010; Shakkottai et al., 2011; Jayabal et al., 2016; Stoyas et al., 2020; Hurlock et al., 2008; Shakkottai et al., 2009; Bosch et al., 2015; Walter et al., 2006; Alviña and Khodakhah, 2010; Ady et al., 2018; Larivière et al., 2019; Cook et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies describing reduced PN firing in various ataxia models.

claim: Complete deficiency of both ATM and APTX was necessary to produce significantly reduced spontaneous Purkinje neuron firing frequency.
source: We found that complete deficiency of both ATM and APTX, consistent with the behavioral results, was necessary to produce a significantly reduced spontaneous PN firing frequency (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figures 4G and H.

claim: Significant age-dependent changes in Purkinje neuron firing frequency were only observed in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice.
source: Significant age-dependent changes in firing frequency were also only observed in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice (Figure 4H), with the most significant decline occurring between P120 and P210 (medial: 50.3±2.4 Hz [n=61] vs. 36.9±2.2 Hz [n=31], t-test, p=0.0006).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of firing frequency data presented in Figure 4H.

claim: The most significant decline in Purkinje neuron firing frequency occurred between P120 and P210 in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice.
source: Significant age-dependent changes in firing frequency were also only observed in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice (Figure 4H), with the most significant decline occurring between P120 and P210 (medial: 50.3±2.4 Hz [n=61] vs. 36.9±2.2 Hz [n=31], t-test, p=0.0006).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of firing frequency data.

claim: No significant difference in Purkinje neuron firing frequency was detected between male and female mice within each genotype.
source: No significant difference in PN firing frequency was detected between male and female mice within each genotype, thus the data were pooled (two-way ANOVA, p>0.3 across all pairwise comparisons; Figure 4—figure supplement 4–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA) of firing frequency data.

claim: No difference in coefficient of variation or CV2 of Purkinje neuron firing was detected across sex, age, or genotype.
source: We compared both the coefficient of variation (CV) and variability in adjacent intervals (CV2) between AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− and control mice (Figure 4—figure supplements 4 and 5). No difference in these parameters across sex, age, or genotype was detected.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of CV and CV2 data presented in supplementary figures.

claim: In A-T patients, ataxia is usually detected between 1 and 2 years of age and is associated with little to no cerebellar atrophy.
source: In A-T patients, ataxia is usually detected between 1 and 2 years of age and is associated with little to no cerebellar atrophy (Tavani et al., 2003; Taylor et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tavani et al., 2003; Taylor et al., 2015, which describe the clinical progression of A-T.

claim: Significant structural changes and atrophy in A-T patients are usually first detected via neuroimaging between 5 and 10 years of age.
source: Significant structural changes and atrophy are usually first detected via neuroimaging between 5 and 10 years of age (Demaerel et al., 1992; Tavani et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Demaerel et al., 1992; Tavani et al., 2003, which describe neuroimaging findings in A-T patients.

claim: The gross size of the cerebellum in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice was normal early in life but significant atrophy developed as ataxia severity increased.
source: In the AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice, we found the gross size of the cerebellum to be normal early in life, but significant atrophy developed as the severity of ataxia increased (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cerebellar size measurements presented in Figure 5A.

claim: At early stages (P45-P210), cerebellar size in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice did not differ from mice with at least one copy of the Atm gene.
source: At early stages (P45–P210), the size of the cerebellum in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice did not differ from mice with at least one copy of the Atm gene (two-way ANOVA, F(3,52)=1.0, p=0.4).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA) of cerebellar size data.

claim: By P210, the overall size of the cerebellum in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice was significantly reduced.
source: However, by P210, the overall size of the cerebellum in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice was significantly reduced (one-way ANOVA, F(3,37)=1.4, p=0.3), with the degenerative process continuing to at least the last time point investigated (P460).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA) of cerebellar size data.

claim: No correlation was found between animal weight and cerebellar size in any genotype at P460.
source: To rule out the possibility that reduced cerebellar size was related to the smaller stature of AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice, we examined, animal weight and cerebellar size and found no correlation (Pearson's correlation, p>0.3 for all four genotypes at P460, n=10–20).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Pearson's correlation) of weight and cerebellar size data.

claim: Cerebellar size did not differ between male and female mice across genotypes at P460.
source: Furthermore, we found that cerebellar size did not differ between male and the on average 22% smaller female mice across genotypes at this age (two-way ANOVA, F(2, 153)=1.9, p=0.2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA) of cerebellar size data.

claim: Cerebellar neurodegeneration in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice begins after P120 and is correlated with ATM and APTX deficiency.
source: Therefore, cerebellar neurodegeneration in the AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice, which begins after P120, is correlated with ATM and APTX deficiency.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the temporal progression of cerebellar atrophy data.

claim: Cerebellar atrophy in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice was associated with selective reduction in molecular layer width.
source: We found cerebellar atrophy to be associated with a selective reduction in the width of the molecular layer (ML) where PN dendrites reside (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological measurements presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Molecular layer width in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice was normal in younger mice but progressively decreased as ataxia severity increased.
source: Consistent with the temporal changes in gross cerebellar size, PN firing frequency, and behavior, ML width in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice was normal in younger mice but progressively decreased in width as the severity of ataxia increased (P400: 120.2±2.1 μm [n=5] vs. 140.2±4.8 μm [n=5], two-way ANOVA, F(1, 42)=45.04, p<0.0001; Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA) of molecular layer width measurements presented in Figure 5B.

claim: No difference in granule cell layer width across age was observed in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice.
source: In contrast, no difference in the width of the granule cell layer (GCL) across age was observed in the AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice (P400: 135.5±2.4 μm [n=6] vs. 127.5±4.3 μm [n=5], two-way ANOVA, F(1, 42)=3.3, p=0.08; Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA) of granule cell layer width measurements.

claim: Cerebellar atrophy was not due to Purkinje neuron cell death, as PN density did not differ between genotypes.
source: Cerebellar atrophy, however, was not due to PN cell death, as PN density did not significantly differ between AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− and Atm+/+; Aptx+/+ mice (P400: 4.5±0.3 [n=9] vs. 4.5±0.2 [n=7] PNs/4000 μm2, Welch's t-test, p=0.9; Figure 5C and D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Welch's t-test) of PN density measurements presented in Figures 5C and D.

claim: No evidence of increased programmed cell death or microglial activation was found in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice.
source: Moreover, we found no evidence from immunohistolological experiments for increased levels of programmed cell death or microglial activation in the AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistological data presented in supplementary figures.

claim: Purkinje neuron somatic size was reduced in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice compared to wild-type.
source: At the anatomical level, we found pathological changes in PN morphology, as somatic size was reduced (15.3±0.3 [n=5] vs. 17.8±0.1 [n=5] μm, Welch's t-test, p=0.0004; Figure 5E) and the primary and secondary dendrites were abnormally large in caliber in the AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice (3.1±0.2 [n=6] vs. 2.8±0.1 [n=6] μm, Welch's t-test, p=0.003; Figure 5F and -Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Welch's t-test) of PN soma measurements presented in Figure 5E.

claim: Primary and secondary dendrites of Purkinje neurons were abnormally large in caliber in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice.
source: At the anatomical level, we found pathological changes in PN morphology, as somatic size was reduced (15.3±0.3 [n=5] vs. 17.8±0.1 [n=5] μm, Welch's t-test, p=0.0004; Figure 5E) and the primary and secondary dendrites were abnormally large in caliber in the AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice (3.1±0.2 [n=6] vs. 2.8±0.1 [n=6] μm, Welch's t-test, p=0.003; Figure 5F and -Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Welch's t-test) of dendrite width measurements presented in Figure 5F.

claim: Chronic sinopulmonary infections associated with immunodeficiency are one of the leading causes of death in A-T patients.
source: Chronic sinopulmonary infections associated with immunodeficiency are one of the leading causes of death in A-T patients (Morrell et al., 1986; Bhatt and Bush, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Morrell et al., 1986; Bhatt and Bush, 2014, which describe causes of death in A-T patients.

claim: Immunodeficiency in A-T is linked to defects in antigen receptor gene rearrangement during B- and T-lymphocyte generation.
source: Immunodeficiency is linked to deficits in the generation of B- and T-lymphocytes that have been linked to defects in the antigen receptor gene rearrangement processes during the generation of these cells in the bone marrow and thymus, respectively (Staples et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Staples et al., 2008, which describes immune defects in A-T.

claim: Defects in mature lymphocyte numbers in A-T include decreases in CD4+ helper T-cells and CD8+ killer T-cells.
source: The resulting defects in mature lymphocyte numbers include decreases in CD4+ helper T-cells and killer CD8+ T-cells (Schubert et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schubert et al., 2002, which describes T-cell defects in A-T.

claim: A significant reduction in the total fraction of CD3+ T-cells was observed in mice with reduced or absent ATM expression.
source: In the peripheral blood, we observed a significant reduction in the total fraction of CD3+ T-cells in mice with reduced or absent ATM expression compared to wild-type mice (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 6.

claim: ATM and APTX deficiencies reduced T-cells in peripheral blood by over 65% compared to wild-type controls.
source: ATM and APTX deficiencies reduced T-cells in peripheral blood by over 65% compared to wild-type controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from the study.

claim: The effect of APTX deficiency on T-cell reduction was additive to that of ATM deficiency.
source: The effect of APTX deficiency was additive to that of ATM deficiency, suggesting a different mechanism of action for each of these two proteins on T-cell generation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the flow cytometry data showing combined effects of ATM and APTX deficiency.

claim: The reduction in T-cells in peripheral blood was mostly associated with reduction in the CD4+ helper T-cell population.
source: The reduction in the percentage of T-cells in peripheral blood was mostly associated with reduction in the CD4+ helper T-cell population (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: The proportion of CD8+ T-cells was increased only in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice.
source: Of interest, the proportion of CD8+ T-cells was increased only in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− and AtmR35X/+; Aptx−/− mice had significantly elevated proportions of CD44+CD25−, CD44+CD25+, and CD44−CD25+ thymocytes compared to wild-type.
source: AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− and AtmR35X/+; Aptx−/− but not AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx+/+ mice had significantly elevated proportions of CD44+CD25−, CD44+CD25+, and CD44−CD25+ cells compared to wildtype (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: The fraction of CD44−CD25− double negative thymocytes from AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− and AtmR35X/+; Aptx−/− mice is significantly lower than wild-type.
source: These increased proportions appear to be due in part to an impediment of CD44−CD25+ cells maturing into CD44−CD25− double negative cells, as the fraction of CD44−CD25− cells from AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− and AtmR35X/+; Aptx−/− mice is significantly lower than wildtype (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: APTX deficiency has the greatest effect on the loss of DN4 thymocytes.
source: Of interest, APTX deficiency by itself had the greatest effect on the loss of DN4 cells, suggesting that APTX deficiency, rather than ATM deficiency, is responsible for this effect.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the flow cytometry data showing effects of APTX deficiency on DN4 cells.

claim: This finding implicates APTX in gene rearrangement during TCRβ recombination for the first time.
source: To our knowledge, this finding implicates for the first time APTX in gene rearrangement during the process of TCRβ recombination.
evidence: The claim is stated as a novel finding from the study based on the thymocyte development data.

claim: ATM-deficient mice displayed decreased expression of CD4+CD8− and CD4−CD8+ single positive thymocytes.
source: In agreement with our results in the blood and prior studies, we found that ATM-deficient mice but not control mice displayed decreased expression of CD4+CD8− and CD4−CD8+ single positive thymocytes (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: ATM expression from one copy of the gene is enough to restore CD4+ deficits in the blood.
source: Importantly, we found that expression of one copy of the ATM gene is enough to restore CD4+ deficits in the blood indicating that therapies able to restore partial ATM expression would have therapeutic efficacy.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the flow cytometry data showing rescue of CD4+ T-cells with one Atm copy.

claim: ATM expression was consistently restored in spleen and cerebellum of AtmR35X and AtmQ35X mice by both G418 and GJ103.
source: In both types of ATM-deficient mice, ATM expression was consistently restored in the spleen and cerebellum by both G418 and GJ103 (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 8.

claim: SMRT compounds can enable read-through of at least two of the three possible nonsense mutations causing PTCs.
source: These results demonstrate that our SMRT compounds can enable read-through of at least two of the three possible nonsense mutations causing PTCs and provide the rationale for in vivo efficacy testing in follow-on studies.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the Western blot data showing ATM restoration with read-through compounds.

claim: The AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mouse model displays the most comprehensive set of A-T symptoms of any model to date.
source: By increasing genotoxic stress through the addition of a secondary hit to the DDR pathway, we generated a novel mouse model that displays the most comprehensive set of A-T symptoms of any model to date.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement of the study's findings comparing this model to prior models.

claim: The three leading causes of premature death in A-T each contribute to roughly a third of deaths.
source: Taken together, these comorbidities encompass the three leading causes of premature death in A-T—each contributing to roughly a third of deaths.
evidence: The claim is based on the study's findings and general knowledge about A-T mortality.

claim: The incapacitating effect of ataxia is the most penetrant symptom and has the greatest impact on A-T patient quality of life.
source: Of these, the incapacitating effect of ataxia is the most penetrant and is reported by patients and caregivers as having the greatest impact on their quality of life.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about A-T patient experiences.

claim: The presence of ataxia and cerebellar atrophy in this mouse model provides the first resource to elucidate mechanisms of neurological dysfunction in A-T.
source: For this reason, the presence of ataxia and cerebellar atrophy in this new mouse model is of great significance, as it provides for the very first time a resource to not only elucidate the mechanisms of neurological dysfunction, but also a critically needed in vivo model to test severely needed A-T therapeutics, such as the read-through compounds we describe here.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion about the significance of the new model.

claim: Several similarities exist between the overall progression of ataxia in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice and A-T patients.
source: We found several similarities between the overall progression of ataxia in the AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice and A-T patients.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement comparing the mouse model to human disease progression.

claim: In clinical A-T, motor deficits are observable by roughly 2 years of age.
source: In clinical A-T, motor deficits are observable by roughly 2 years of age, when parents and doctors detect a lowered ability to transition from toddling to a smooth, reflexively coordinated gate—unfortunately, little is known about motor defects at earlier stages due to the diseases low prevalence and current lack of early diagnostic testing (Rothblum-Oviatt et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rothblum-Oviatt et al., 2016, which describes clinical progression of A-T.

claim: A-T patients usually learn to walk without assistance and neurological symptoms tend to remain stable through the first 4-5 years of life.
source: Patients usually learn to walk without assistance and neurological symptoms tend to remain stable through the first 4–5 years of life (Rothblum-Oviatt et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rothblum-Oviatt et al., 2016, which describes clinical progression of A-T.

claim: The severity of late-developing ataxia was variable in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice, similar to A-T patients.
source: We also found, similar to A-T patients, that the severity of the late-developing ataxia was variable, with some mice ambulating with a clumsy, high-stepping rear gate (Video 3) and others moving almost entirely via contortion of the rear trunk (Figure 1E and Video 4; Rothblum-Oviatt et al., 2016; Levy and Lang, 2018; Boder and Sedgwick, 1958).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral observations and citations describing variability in A-T patients.

claim: Loss of motor coordination in A-T has been attributed to cerebellar degeneration due to its relatively selective neuropathology.
source: The loss of motor coordination in A-T has been attributed to cerebellar degeneration due to its relatively selective neuropathology across the brain and its causal role in several different forms of ataxia (Hoche et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hoche et al., 2012, which discusses cerebellar pathology in ataxia.

claim: Cerebellar size in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice is initially normal but progressively atrophies concurrently with changes in neurological function, consistent with A-T patient neuroimaging studies.
source: Consistent with A-T patient neuroimaging studies (Wallis et al., 2007; Sahama et al., 2015; Sahama et al., 2014; Dineen et al., 2020; Tavani et al., 2003; Quarantelli et al., 2013), we find that cerebellar size in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice is initially normal, but progressively atrophies concurrently with changes in neurological function.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and citations to neuroimaging studies in A-T patients.

claim: It is unclear from clinical data if ataxia severity is a good predictor of the extent of cerebellar degeneration found postmortem in A-T patients.
source: While loss of cerebellar tissue has been considered a main cause of ataxia in humans, it is unclear from clinical data if ataxia severity is a good predictor of the extent of cerebellar degeneration found postmortem (Aguilar et al., 1968; Crawford et al., 2006; Dineen et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to clinical studies examining the relationship between ataxia and cerebellar pathology.

claim: Changes in cerebellar function itself, rather than profound loss of cerebellar cells, are sufficient to cause the ataxic phenotype in AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice.
source: Our histological observations in the AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice suggest that changes in cerebellar function itself, rather than profound loss of cerebellar cells, are sufficient to cause the ataxic phenotype, consistent with the observation of behavioral defects prior to significant PN loss in several SCAs (Shakkottai et al., 2011; Lorenzetti et al., 2000; Clark et al., 1997; Jayabal et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the histological data, supported by citations to similar findings in other ataxia models.

claim: The rodent brain may more flexibly utilize compensatory pathways or redundant proteins while responding to DNA lesions.
source: One possibility is that the rodent brain may more flexibly utilize compensatory pathways or redundant proteins while responding to the ~15k DNA lesions that impact cells each day (Lindahl and Barnes, 2000).
evidence: The claim is speculation about why double mutation is needed in mice, supported by a citation about DNA damage frequency.

claim: Deficiency in ATM or APTX alone may not adequately impact cell health during the mouse's comparatively short lifespan.
source: Alternatively, it may be the case that deficiency in ATM or APTX alone does not adequately impact cell health during the mouse's comparatively short lifespan, and thus eliminating both proteins is necessary to achieve sufficient accumulation of DNA damage to manifest over this time period.
evidence: The claim is speculation about why double mutation is needed in mice.

claim: ATM and APTX have distinct biochemical properties and functional roles in the DNA damage response.
source: This possibility is strengthened by the fact that ATM and APTX have distinct biochemical properties and functional roles in the DDR, and therefore deficiency in both would be predicted to cause a broader, additive hit to genome stability than either alone (i.e., increased genotoxic stress).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ATM and APTX functions.

claim: The finding that two genome stability pathway proteins are required to induce neurological defects in mice strongly suggests it is the loss of ATM's role in DNA repair that causes cerebellar defects.
source: Our finding that two genome stability pathway proteins are required to induce neurological defects in mice strongly suggests that it is the loss of ATM's role in DNA repair, rather than potential functions in oxidative stress signaling, mitophagy, or mitochondrial function that cause the cerebellar defects (Shiloh, 2020).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the study's findings, supported by a citation discussing ATM functions.

claim: APTX has been observed within the mitochondria of brain cells where it is thought to support processing of mitochondrial DNA.
source: Alternatives, however, cannot be completely ruled out, as APTX, like ATM, has been observed within the mitochondria of brain cells, where it is thought to support the processing of mitochondrial DNA (Meagher and Lightowlers, 2014; Sykora et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Meagher and Lightowlers, 2014; Sykora et al., 2011, which describe APTX localization and function.

claim: The biophysical perturbations observed in Purkinje neurons from AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice are similarly found in several other mouse models of ataxia.
source: The biophysical perturbations observed in PNs recorded from the AtmR35X/R35X; Aptx−/− mice are similarly found in several other mouse models of ataxia.
evidence: The claim is a comparison of findings to other ataxia models.

claim: Changes in PN input resistance, membrane capacitance, and AP threshold and width have been described in mouse models of SCA 1, 3, and 7.
source: This includes changes we observed in PN input resistance, membrane capacitance, and AP threshold and width, which have also been described in mouse models of SCA like 1, 3, and 7 (Stoyas et al., 2020; Shakkottai et al., 2011; Dell'Orco et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies describing similar findings in other ataxia models.

claim: Progressive reduction in PN AP firing frequency is reported in a large number of ataxic mouse models.
